A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LSFS research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite the AIOS retitling and relocated material.

before.justification: Sections 5.1–5.3 report original parser-accuracy, retrieval, rollback and file-sharing experiments; appendices provide additional case analyses.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, supplemented by supervisor measurements, participant timing results, confirmation ablations and parser-retry experiments.

M1.justification: Appendix H.1 explicitly introduces failure-informed re-prompting followed by a second parsing attempt. The vector-index architecture, embedding model, syscalls and APIs remain unchanged; Appendix G mainly elaborates safeguards already described in v2.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds a file-operation study involving 10 Ph.D. students, and Section 5.2 newly evaluates supervisor handling of file updates. These extend evaluated populations and tasks within the existing file-management domain. Increasing retrieval to 120 files is a scale change, not a new dataset.

E2.justification: Appendix F adds a timed comparison against manual Linux-command workflows, including rollback, grouping and joining operations. The existing semantic-retrieval, keyword-search and file-sharing comparator sets are retained; added related-work citations do not introduce evaluated LLM baselines.

E3.justification: Semantic retrieval gains a 120-file condition, while supervisor testing covers 100–1600 files. New protocols measure participants' time by workflow stage, compare confirmation enabled versus disabled, and retry previously failed parser cases. These substantially expand evaluation design without establishing that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test supervisor scalability, the contribution of user confirmation to preventing mistakes, recovery from parsing failures, and the sources of user-operation time. The earlier rollback analysis, semantic-retrieval case study and file-sharing failure examples remain, with the latter two relocated to Appendices I and K.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, uncertainty intervals, error bars or significance tests for its experiments. The new participant counts and corrective second parsing attempts describe evaluation protocols rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds 120-file results: LSFS accuracy is 92.9%, versus 35.2% and 63.8% without LSFS for Gemini and GPT-4o-mini respectively. New tables report supervisor latency of 0.6–4.4 ms, workflow totals of 27.59 versus 212.16 seconds, zero retrieval errors after confirmation, and conditional second-pass parsing success. Original retrieval rows, keyword-search scores, rollback curves and relocated file-sharing scores are retained.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal mathematical theory, assumptions or proofs. The new operational-complexity table compares command workflows rather than introducing a mathematical complexity analysis.

C1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction now explicitly position LSFS as providing semantic file-management services for AIOS. The central contributions concerning semantic indexing, reusable interfaces, natural-language parsing and safeguards, together with the headline performance claims, remain.

C2.justification: New interpretations attribute parser failures to LLM capability and randomness, argue that corrective parsing usually suffices within two attempts, and explain why time savings persist without command-learning time. Supervisor efficiency and confirmation-based safety also receive new interpretation. Existing applicability limits and future directions are retained in Appendix J.

D1.justification: Appendices G–H newly specify two confirmations for file changes, the corrective retry prompt, and instruction collection from 10 Ph.D. students followed by test-based refinement and selection. These add implementation and data-provenance information. Existing API parameters, LlamaIndex usage, embedding-model disclosure and code-access link remain.

R1.justification: AIOS, already cited in v2, becomes the explicit foundation for LSFS. Sections 2.2–2.3 add references concerning reasoning, general LLMs, coding and recommendation, and replace the Iyer citation with Lawrence and Riezler. The principal positioning against earlier semantic file systems and parsers remains.

P1.justification: The title, authorship, affiliations and publication header change, alongside localized introduction, related-work and explanatory edits. File-sharing evaluation moves to Appendix H.2 and future directions to Appendix J, but the main section sequence and most existing prose remain.

P2.justification: New Tables 3 and 8–11 substantially expand the displays of supervisor costs, command workflows, participant timings, safety and parser recovery. Table 2 gains two rows, and the file-sharing table moves from the main text to Appendix H.2 as Table 12. Existing figures are retained, with the parser and workflow figures relocated and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v3 extends scalability testing and supplies direct usability and confirmation-ablation evidence missing from v2, while retaining the earlier findings. These additions improve empirical support, but sparse study details, absent uncertainty estimates and test-based prompt selection disclosed in Appendix H.1 limit their strength. The net improvement is useful but limited.
